The Siamese mud carp Henicorhynchus siamensis is a small cyprinid endemic to the Mekong Basin, where it supports one of the region's most important artisanal fisheries. Field surveys conducted throughout its range indicate that this species exhibits a maximum recorded total length of 26.4 centimeters [Li = 26.4 centimeters], a modest size typical of trophic generalists in highly seasonal floodplain systems. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from individuals maintained at a constant water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] yielded a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 18.6% [GSI = 18.6%]. This relatively moderate index suggests that the species allocates a significant but not extreme proportion of its body mass toward ovarian development, a pattern consistent with an iteroparous reproductive strategy in which females spawn multiple times over several months during the monsoon-driven flood pulse.

Longitudinal mark-recapture studies have provided detailed size-at-maturity data for this species. The total length at which 50 percent of individuals exhibit macroscopic gonadal development, a standard proxy for the onset of puberty, is estimated at 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters]. This length corresponds closely to a wet weight at puberty of 76.4 grams [Wwp = 76.4 grams], a body mass that is reached during the second or third wet season for most individuals. The relationship between length and mass follows a predicted power function derived from local population samples, allowing robust estimates of condition across different hydrological years. Achieving this pubertal size threshold appears to be a prerequisite for initiating vitellogenesis and the subsequent cascade of reproductive events that culminate in spawning.

Newly fertilized ova in this species are demersal and adhesive, with a mean diameter of approximately 0.9 millimeters. From this diameter, the computed wet weight at birth, defined here as the mass of the freshly fertilised ovum, is approximately 0.00038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00038 grams]. This minute initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo, which must transition to exogenous feeding rapidly following chorion rupture. In laboratory rearing trials conducted at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the yolk-sac larva stage was observed to persist for only two to three days post-eclosion, after which mouth opening and first exogenous feeding commenced. The minimal maternal investment per offspring is typical of highly fecund, broadcast-spawning cyprinids that produce large numbers of small pelagic eggs.

As individuals approach the upper end of the size distribution, their body mass stabilizes at an ultimate wet weight of 176 grams [Wwi = 176 grams]. This asymptotic mass is predicted from the species-specific length-weight relationship and has been confirmed through repeated sampling of large-bodied adults from the Tonle Sap floodplain. The ultimate total length of 26.4 centimeters [Li = 26.4 centimeters] therefore anchors a maximum body mass that is substantially greater than the pubertal threshold, indicating that a considerable period of post-pubertal somatic growth separates first maturity from the attainment of maximal size. This decoupling of reproductive and somatic trajectories is a common life-history pattern among medium-sized cyprinids inhabiting unpredictable tropical river systems, where survival and growth rates vary markedly with annual flood intensity.

The maximum longevity of Henicorhynchus siamensis has been inferred from both otolith annulus counts and tag-return data across several Mekong tributaries. Under the prevailing thermal regime characterized by an average water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the species attains a maximum lifespan of approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years]. The gonadosomatic index was 18.6% [GSI = 18.6%], measured at the same temperature at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. Such a suite of life-history parameters—small ultimate size, early maturation at 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters] total length, brief lifespan, and modest gonadal investment—positions this species as a classic opportunist, well suited to the boom-and-bust productivity cycles of large tropical floodplain rivers.
